newsitem.title: USA: Swiss banks face second Holocaust suit.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks face second Holocaust suit.

text.p: A second class action lawsuit has been filed against a group of Swiss banks on behalf of Nazi Holocaust survivors and families of victims trying to recover assets taken from Jews during the Second World War.

The latest suit, filed in Brooklyn federal court on Monday, was brought on behalf of five plaintiffs living in New York, California, Britain and Canada. It seeks disgorgement of unspecified amounts and damages to be determined at trial.
Defendants in the suit are the Swiss Bank Corp., Union Bank of Switzerland and Credit Suisse.
Marty Mendelsohn, the Washington, D.C. lawyer who filed the more than 100-page suit, said the plaintiffs were seeking a court order forcing the banks to supply an accounting of the missing assets.

Earlier this month, Gizella Weisshaus a Romanian Holocaust survivor living in Brooklyn, filed a $20 billion class action suit on behalf of all Holocaust victims and survivors who had deposited money and property in Swiss banks for safe keeping until after the war.
The Nazis also stripped class members of personal property including the gold from their teeth, both suits say.
The suits allege that the banks took control of, bought, converted or transferred these assets through transactions or agreements with the Nazi government during the war.

On Wednesday, a Swiss historian made public documents showing that unclaimed accounts of Holocaust victims were used to ease Switzerland's postwar compensation disputes with Poland and Hungary under secret agreements.

Also Wednesday, a previously secret U.S. army document was released showing that Allied soldiers found bags of gold fillings from human teeth in a Nazi cache in western Germany at the end of the Second World War.
The document said the Nazi cache of gold, jewels and cash was found by U.S. forces at the Kaiseroda salt mine at Merkers on April 8, 1945.

World Jewish Congress President Edgar Bronfman released the document at a meeting of Jewish community leaders in which he gave an update on negotiations with Switzerland over return of assets from Holocaust victims that may still be in Swiss banks.
